situation: Registration for an upcoming event is much lower than expected.  You had hopes that it would be well attended, and there’s only one week left before it starts.
Your team wants to start promoting an event early to build interest, but several important event details are still changing and may not be finalized for a while.
Shortly after publishing a social media post, someone points out that it contains a technical error that could mislead readers.
A utility client needs to approve an EDA project’s case study before it goes out, but they're slow to respond and the deadline is approaching.
You’re given a technical report packed with acronyms, technical language, and dense data and asked to turn it into marketing content that a general audience can understand.
A utility representative has repeatedly given participants guidance that appears inconsistent with the program’s expectations, creating the potential for customer confusion.
At an outreach event, a customer tells you they were dissatisfied with a previous experience participating in the EDA program and is clearly frustrated about what happened.

Over time, a team member has submitted several questions to an internal discussion forum – which seem related to program procedures, but the questions are vague enough on specifics to make the questions hard to answer.
A report for a utility client is due tomorrow, your calendar includes several hours of meetings, and two additional leadership requests arrive that also appear important and time-sensitive.

A hard-to-schedule customer requests an intro tomorrow with a specific consultant. The consultant’s calendar appears open, but they’ve been in meetings all day and haven’t yet responded about tomorrow’s availability.

During the EDA process, a project has been discussed exclusively through an owner’s rep, who handles all communication with the owner. The project now requires a document signed directly by the owner, but the consultant has stopped responding to follow-up requests.
A customer is uncomfortable sending a W-9 and raises privacy concerns, even though the document is required for participation and eventual incentive processing.

A customer submits a W-9 that appears complete, but the utility reports that it fails validation and cannot be used for incentive payment. The customer insists the form is correct and is frustrated by the delay.

A project is nearing construction completion, but the only project contact has stopped responding after months of outreach and may have left the company. Project documentation needed for verification still hasn’t been received.
One consultant’s completion dates look correct in the Coop but show up as one day later in exported reports. Other users are unaffected, making the problem inconsistent and difficult to reproduce.

A bug in NEO initially looks like a quick fix that can fit into the current release, but QA uncovers deeper problems requiring substantially more work and putting the release timeline at risk … and delaying the fix could result in incorrect model results.

A critical feature depends on a third-party service that begins failing intermittently. The third-party provider offers no useful status update or support response, while the app’s users continue relying on a now-buggy application.

The Silent Deploy: A production update goes out Friday afternoon that includes a routine update to an underlying software component. Everything looks fine until Monday, when a user reports intermittent errors in a feature that wasn't changed. No one called attention to the component update during review, and its role in the problem is unclear.

The Competing Priorities Standoff: Two project leads both need the same backend developer at full capacity this week — one for a client demo, one for a security patch with a compliance deadline. Neither will budge, and the developer is caught in the middle.

A senior developer leaves the company. Weeks later, a problem reveals that a critical process everyone thought was documented actually depended on a manual workaround that only the former developer knew to perform.

A new vendor sends us their first invoice, but the vendor has not yet been set up in Willdan’s payment systems so their invoice cannot be processed yet, and the due date on the invoice is rapidly approaching.

An office maintenance issue needs attention, and you learn that the repair work will likely be noisy and otherwise disruptive to the office team while it’s being carried out. Several staff meetings are already on the calendar during that time.
A couple hours before an all-hands meeting, you learn that the lunch order was lost by the caterer and they won’t have the order ready until later that afternoon.
An employee is unable to charge hours to the timesheet code associated with their work, and Costpoint keeps giving them errors.
A program manager needs work on a new project to begin as soon as possible, but the project has not yet been established for time charging, billing, and financial tracking.

A utility client contacts Finance questioning why a particular project milestone appeared on a recent invoice, even though Finance billed according to information previously provided by the program team.
A program manager asks Finance to bill an expense, but it is unclear which charge number it belongs to. Based on experience, you have a strong guess about which number was intended.
While reviewing project finances, you notice that a project is approaching the end of its available contract funding even though work is still underway.
After an invoice has already been submitted for monthly processing, a program manager discovers that important information on it needs to change.

You’ve scheduled a verification site visit with the design team lead and building owner. You arrive at the scheduled time and construction is still underway. You wait by the main entrance but don’t see anyone ‘in charge’, it is now 15 minutes past the scheduled time, and your project contact isn’t answering their phone.

After a project is complete, you review all the documentation and submittals we’ve received … but there’s no information on several measures you were expecting to see. Those strategies might have been implemented, but you aren’t able to confirm one way or the other.

The EEPS team has been requesting submittals for months without any luck. The owner says they don’t have the time to track down the documentation, and they say Willdan will have to do a site visit to verify everything.

You review the drawings for a project that we thought had completed construction - but you find that only half of the expected buildings are done and the remaining buildings are now “Phase 2” construction and won’t be done for another year.
A building owner from a project completed six months ago calls because actual utility bills are higher than they expected based on the verification report and wants to know what’s happening.
During verification, you find that several energy-saving strategies were not implemented and the project’s verified savings now fall just below the threshold required to receive an incentive.
During verification, the actual building areas differ substantially from what was modeled, with individual areas varying in both directions and the total area about 10% higher than expected.
After sending a draft verification report, you discover that you used the wrong baseline and overstated the performance of a cooling strategy that is actually only at baseline efficiency.
Shortly after emailing a Draft Verification Report to a design team, you realize that you accidentally attached the report for a completely different project with different participants.
You are prepared for a scheduled project-team Webex meeting, but ten minutes after the start time no one else has joined and none of the expected participants has contacted you.
During a results meeting, an owner’s representative stops the discussion and says the analysis cannot be accurate because the model does not reflect their exact equipment specifications.
An energy model crashes repeatedly, and troubleshooting takes much longer than expected. The project will not be ready for third-party review until the day before the scheduled results meeting.
A project team seemed engaged during the intro call but has not responded to any emails or phone calls for five months despite repeated attempts to reconnect.

After you model the three HVAC options the project team requested, the mechanical engineer announces during the results meeting that the design has changed and none of the modeled scenarios is still valid.
Your energy model is nearly complete when the project team announces that the entire building layout has changed, affecting much of the work already performed.
During an intro call, the mechanical engineer describes a new system their firm developed that your modeling tool cannot represent directly.
During a results meeting, a utility account representative suggests several potentially useful design changes that were not included in the energy model being presented.
After presenting results to the project team, you discover that a copy-and-paste error affected multiple modeled scenarios and most of the results you shared were incorrect.
A design team leaves you off its updated drawing distribution, so you unknowingly model outdated plans and discover the problem only when meeting with the team to review your findings.
Updated drawings are uploaded to the wrong project folder, and you complete the energy model using outdated plans before discovering the newer files.
